[[File:Kushiiwamado-jinja ichinotorii.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|First torii}}]]
'''Kushiiwamado Shrine''' (くしいわまどじんじゃ) is a Shinto shrine in Fukui, Tamba-Sasayama, Hyogo. It is an Engishiki Meishin-taisha shrine (two seats) and was formerly ranked as a prefectural shrine.

=== Enshrined deities ===
; Main deity
* {{ill|Ama-no-Iwato-wake no Kami|ja|天石門別神|zh|天石門別神|qid=Q10940542|lt=Kushiiwamado-no-Mikoto}}
; Co-enshrined
* {{ill|Ama-no-Iwato-wake no Kami|ja|天石門別神|zh|天石門別神|qid=Q10940542|lt=Toyoiwamado-no-Mikoto}}
* Omiyahime-no-Mikoto

=== About the deities ===
Kushiiwamado and Toyoiwamado are known in classical texts as gate-guardian deities. In the ''Kojiki,'' they appear as alternate names of Ame-no-Iwato-wake-no-kami, described as "deities of the gate." In ''Kogo Shui,'' they guard the palace gates after Amaterasu's relocation. The Engishiki also lists them among palace gate deities. Their exact historical relation to this shrine remains unclear, though Edo scholarship linked this shrine as their principal cult site.

=== History ===
The ''Shinsho Gecchokufu-sho'' (806) records five households of shrine endowment for "Kushiiwamado deity" in Tanba Province, the earliest textual attestation.

In the ''Engishiki Jinmyocho'' (927), it appears as "Kushiiwamado Shrine, two seats, both Meishin-taisha" in Taki District, Tanba Province. The shrine preserves transmission of three Heian-period deity statues (Important Cultural Properties).

In medieval records it appears as "Oimo-sha." After repeated war damage post-Onin War, it was rebuilt in 1567; it was later burned again during warfare in the Tensho era and lost much of its shrine lands. In early modern times, buildings were reconstructed (records exist for 1663 honden work and 1775 haiden work). It was known as "Kushiiwamado Daimyojin" and had a shrine-temple called Omiya-ji.

In 1873 it was ranked village shrine; in 1904 it was promoted to prefectural shrine.

=== Precinct ===
[[File:Kushiiwamado-jinja honden-2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|{{center|Honden}}]]
The current honden dates to 1959. A sacred spring once called "Fukui" stood near the shrine and is said to be the origin of the place-name. Behind the shrine is a hill called Miyayama with a sacred rock (iwakura), regarded as a remnant of ancient ritual practice.

File:Kushiiwamado-jinja miyayama-2.jpg|Miyayama hill and shrine grove

=== Cultural properties ===
=== Important Cultural Properties (National) ===
* Wooden seated statue of Kushi-Iwado deity
* Wooden seated statue of Toyo-Iwado deity
* Wooden seated statue of Omiyahime deity
(All from the Heian period; designated April 17, 1911)

The first two statues were stolen sometime between December 1981 and April 1982.

=== Site information ===
* Address: Fukui 1170, Tamba-Sasayama, Hyogo
* Access: Wing Shinki bus to "Tamba Omiya" stop, then immediately nearby
